title: Self-Sampling Can Be Feasible for Respiratory Infections - Medscape

analysis.time: The study was conducted from May to September 2023, with results published online on July 29, 2026. The first symptoms were reported during the first month of the study.
analysis.location_and_population: The study was conducted in 108 households in Switzerland, including 161 adults, 32 children, 29 cats, and 15 dogs.
analysis.event: A pilot study evaluated the feasibility of self-sampling for respiratory infections, including human metapneumovirus, in a Swiss household cohort. The study involved participants collecting nasal swabs for testing and using online questionnaires to report symptoms.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among index cases, 63% of samples were positive for any of the 13 respiratory viruses, with human metapneumovirus being one of the tested pathogens. Potential within-household transmission was observed for human metapneumovirus (as part of the broader respiratory viruses tested).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was published as a short communication in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases. It reported the feasibility of decentralized household-based surveillance for respiratory infections, including human metapneumovirus, but noted limitations such as missing samples and lack of testing for bacterial pathogens.

analysis.brief_en: A pilot study conducted in 108 Swiss households from May to September 2023 explored the feasibility of self-sampling for respiratory infections, including human metapneumovirus. Participants collected nasal swabs for testing, and online questionnaires were used to report symptoms. The study found that 63% of index case samples were positive for any of the 13 respiratory viruses tested, with human metapneumovirus being one of them. Potential within-household transmission was observed for several viruses, including human metapneumovirus. The study, published online on July 29, 2026, in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases, highlighted the viability of decentralized surveillance but noted limitations such as missing samples and the absence of bacterial pathogen testing. The findings support the use of remote sampling and telemedicine for pandemic preparedness, though further research is needed to confirm the specific role of human metapneumovirus in transmission and disease.

title: Q&A: Which Hospitalized Children With RTIs Face the Highest Severe Disease Risk? - Physician's Weekly

analysis.time: The study was conducted between July 2022 and June 2023, with the article published on August 7, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The study was conducted at The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, Ontario, and BC Children’s Hospital in Vancouver, British Columbia, involving 2,585 hospitalized children with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs).
analysis.event: A retrospective study found that more than one in five hospitalized children with acute RTIs developed severe disease, with children transferred from a referring hospital facing the highest risk. The study also identified chronic conditions and age groups as significant risk factors for severe outcomes.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Severe illness occurred in 551 children (21.3%), with 37 (6.7%) deaths. Risk factors included transfer from a referring hospital, chronic conditions, and age groups under 1 year or over 10 years. Viral coinfections were common but not associated with increased severity.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was published in JAMA Network Open, and the findings suggest that viral identification may inform risk but clinical management should focus on the patient’s overall trajectory. Preventive measures, including vaccination and RSV-targeted strategies, are recommended for high-risk patients.

analysis.brief_en: A retrospective study conducted at two Canadian pediatric centers, The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto and BC Children’s Hospital in Vancouver, analyzed 2,585 hospitalized children with acute respiratory tract infections (RTIs) between July 2022 and June 2023. The study found that more than one in five children developed severe disease, with those transferred from a referring hospital facing the highest risk. Chronic conditions, particularly neurologic, developmental, and genetic disorders, were strongly associated with increased severity. Viral coinfections were common but not linked to worse outcomes. Severe illness occurred in 21.3% of cases, with 6.7% of patients dying. The findings emphasize the importance of focusing on patient-specific risk factors rather than the viral pathogen alone, and highlight the need for targeted prevention and early supportive care for high-risk children. The study was published in JAMA Network Open, and its results suggest that clinicians should remain vigilant for nonrespiratory complications, such as cardiac dysfunction and septic shock, particularly in children with worsening clinical status.
